nutshell: Clothes-changing person ReID (CC-ReID) datasets typically only have 2-5 clothing outfits per subject, which limits how well models can learn clothes-invariant identity features. DLCR expands training data by using an off-the-shelf diffusion inpainting model, guided by LLM/VLM-generated clothing text prompts and a human-parsing mask that protects identity-relevant regions (face, hair, body shape), to synthesize ~10x more clothes-changed images per subject, then trains on this expanded data with a progressive schedule and refines predictions at test time via query augmentation.
contributions: First diffusion-based (rather than GAN-based) data expansion pipeline for CC-ReID: a human-parsing mask isolates only clothing regions for inpainting, LLaVA extracts per-image clothing descriptions and LLaMA summarizes/cleans them into one holistic text prompt per clothes-ID, which conditions a frozen, off-the-shelf Stable Diffusion Inpainting model - no fine-tuning of any generative or language component, and the same pipeline is reused unmodified across all 5 datasets (unlike prior GAN methods, which need a separate generator trained per dataset).

A progressive learning schedule during training that gradually widens the pool of generated clothing variants sampled per image (via 4 fixed partitions introduced every N=5 epochs) instead of exposing the full 10x generated diversity from the start.

A test-time prediction refinement strategy: the query image itself is augmented into l clothes-swapped variants, each retrieves its own top-m gallery matches, and the similarity scores are ensembled - a backbone-agnostic inference trick usable regardless of the underlying ReID model.

Releases 2.1M+ generated images (4 of 5 datasets; LTCC withheld for licensing) plus code, and shows the generated data alone improves not just CC-ReID-specific models but also standard (non-clothes-aware) ReID models like PCB/MGN/HPM by large margins (Table 3), with the full pipeline setting new SOTA on 3 of 4 benchmarks using CAL as the backbone.
deficiencies: The key claim motivating the progressive learning strategy - that naively concatenating all generated data at once hurts training - is asserted in the main text but the supporting ablation is pushed entirely to supplementary material, so this core methodological choice isn't actually substantiated with numbers in the paper itself.

Results are inconsistent across datasets: gains are large on PRCC (+11.3 Top-1) and CCVID (+6.3) but small on LTCC (+1.8), where DLCR is also beaten outright by CCFA (45.3 vs. 41.3 Top-1); the paper 'hypothesizes' DLCR would help CCFA too but never tests this since CCFA's code isn't public, leaving the LTCC underperformance unexplained rather than investigated.

There's no quantitative analysis of the diffusion inpainting's own failure modes - e.g. what fraction of the 2.1M generated images actually preserve identity/pose fidelity, whether the human-parsing masks (themselves an imperfect off-the-shelf model) introduce corrupted training samples, or garment photorealism - the only evidence offered is a handful of qualitative examples in Figure 1.

Table 3's headline 'DLCR helps every model' claim mixes the effect of adding generated data with large architectural differences across the six tested backbones (PCB, MGN, HPM, CAL, AIM, GEFF), so the reported 12-30% top-1 swings can't be cleanly attributed to data expansion alone versus each architecture's differing capacity to exploit the extra clothing diversity.
notable: The K=10 generated clothing variants per image are produced by sampling target clothes IDs from *within the same training dataset* (not an open vocabulary of garments), so the '10x clothing diversity' increase is bounded by the combinatorics of clothes IDs already present in that dataset rather than genuinely novel outfits - worth knowing since it caps how much true out-of-distribution diversity this method can add versus, say, generating from open text prompts. Also notable: both the diffusion model and the LLaVA/LLaMA prompt-extraction pipeline run entirely frozen/pretrained (no fine-tuning anywhere), and the whole generation stage runs at roughly 1 image/sec, which is a meaningfully cheap regime worth reusing for other data-scarce fine-grained recognition tasks beyond ReID.
